item.title: A Better Way to Face Challenges and Find the Submarine
item.description:
Education

A Better Way to Face Challenges and Find the Submarine

Approach life challenges like learning how to calm a baby.

Posted October 21, 2026

Key points
  • Most science works like a courtroom, handing down a final yes or no verdict on whether an idea is true.
  • A better way is to treat knowledge like a search, starting with a guess and updating it with more evidence.
  • It's how you soothe a crying baby and how searchers found a lost submarine.

When was the last time you were handed a problem with no instruction manual? Examples: A new job in which nobody explains how things work; your own body when it does something unwelcome.

My nominee for an acute problem: A baby who will not stop crying. How did you solve it?

I bet it was not by demanding proof. You tried and watched. The rocking helped a little; the singing helped a lot. You kept what seemed to work. If you had insisted on certainty before you acted, the baby would still be crying.

A messy, humble, incremental way of learning like that is not a failure. It is how learning works. But a large part of the scientific establishment has spent a century pretending otherwise.

The verdict habit

Most research is conducted this way: You assume that nothing is happening. The new treatment does nothing. No outside assumptions allowed; they will compromise the data. You assume you know nothing.

You gather data and ask: Is this result enough to force me to abandon that assumption if I assume nothing but chance is operating? If yes, the finding is declared real. If no, it goes in the bin.

This may be courtroom mentality. The defendant is presumed innocent, and the study is the trial. The verdict is binary and final. Every trial starts with the jury's memory wiped. What was learned last time doesn't count. The 40 studies that came before don't prove a thing; a treatment that helped some people in some circumstances gets filed away as ineffective.

Finding the submarine

In May 1968, the American nuclear submarine Scorpion vanished in the Atlantic with 99 people aboard.

The government handed the problem to U.S. Navy chief scientist John Craven. He had one search ship. He did what you do with the crying baby, only more carefully.

He divided the ocean into squares and numbered each square. He asked veteran submarine commanders to guess which number contained the sub. Where might it have gone down, and why? He let them bet on their scenarios, sometimes even with bottles of scotch.

Every time the ship swept a square and found nothing, that empty square was not a failure. It lowered the chance for that square and raised it for the others. The map moved and the votes changed. He searched again where the map now said to look.

In late October, the ship found the submarine about 460 miles southwest of the Azores.

The same idea worked on the Air France 447 wreck, lost between Rio and Paris in 2009. Two years of searching turned up nothing. A team of mathematicians took those failures, treated every empty pass as a clue, not a dead end. They redrew the map. The next search found the plane in a week.

These searchers knew the submarine was somewhere. They did not throw away a search because it was empty. They started with their best guess, let reality push the guess around, and got a little less wrong every day.

Just a little bit of science

Statisticians have a long and sometimes bitter argument about whether science should work like the courtroom or the search. I won't drag you into it or use geeky words; that is exactly what has kept people from realizing they already know the answer.

The search says: Knowledge is a map of how confident we are in our guesses; old evidence stays on the map and new evidence moves it. A study that finds nothing still tells you something. Disagreement is allowed, and two people who disagree can still share their findings.

The verdict produces winners and losers. An idea gets convicted or acquitted, and a field spends decades relitigating instead of learning.

We are not clones. What helps your neighbor may not help you, and what helped you last year may not help you now. A verdict about the average person cannot tell you that. A map that you keep updating for this person, in this life, can. The way you figured out your baby is the way a good clinician figures out a client. If we are wise, we will make progress on the rest.

Where this lands

We are living through a period of large, moving, and unfamiliar challenges—climate, fractured communities, and changing technologies. Nobody has the manual. Waiting for proof before we act is a recipe for standing still while the water rises. Pretending to be certain when we aren’t is like driving off a cliff with confidence.

The alternative is humbler. Make your best guess. Say it out loud. Act on it, and let what happens change the guess. Treat the things that did not work as clues. Pool all the maps.

That is how you soothe a crying baby and find a lost submarine. In one square of ocean at a time, we might find our way through what we are facing. You already know how to do this; you've been doing it your whole life. The only truly new step is to stop apologizing for it.

item.title: Why Dating Feels Exhausting
item.description:
Relationships

Why Dating Feels Exhausting

An evolutionary look at why swiping wears us out.

Posted October 21, 2026

Key points
  • Dating app burnout is common, and a mismatch between our evolved minds and endless choice may help explain it.
  • When people see many partners, they become more rejecting and lean on traits they can judge immediately.
  • A profile cannot predict chemistry, which tends to be clear only once people meet.

Have you ever closed a dating app feeling more tired than when you opened it? If you have, you are in good company. In 2024, a survey of 1,000 Americans who used a dating app in the past year found that 78% said they sometimes, often, or always felt emotionally, mentally, or physically exhausted by the apps. Research supports this finding. A study of dating app users by Sharabi and colleagues (2026) found that emotional exhaustion increased over time, as did inefficacy, the sense that one’s efforts are not paying off. Users who self-reported higher levels of depression, anxiety, or loneliness were more prone to both.

The industry is under strain, too. Earlier this month, Bumble agreed to be acquired by Ithaca Holdings for $1.3 billion, far below the roughly $14 billion valuation it carried when it went public in 2021. The number of paying users has declined dramatically; in spring 2026, it had about 16% fewer paying users than a year earlier.

As an evolutionary psychologist, I find this exhaustion intriguing, and I think it stems from mismatch. The term mismatch refers to what happens when psychological mechanisms that evolved in one environment meet inputs far more numerous or intense than those our ancestors are hypothesized to have encountered. These mismatches can result in behavior that no longer serves us well (Li et al., 2018). While I cannot say with total certainty what our ancestral courtship involved, I am confident that it did not entail reviewing hundreds of strangers’ photographs in a single evening in the hopes of finding a mate.

This mismatch between human nature and dating apps explains four reasons dating may feel exhausting.

1. More options make us pickier

In 2004, psychologist Barry Schwartz popularized the idea of a paradox of choice: that having more options can leave us less satisfied. A great demonstration of this paradox is a grocery-store study in which approximately 30% of shoppers who stopped at a display of 6 jams went on to buy one, compared with only 3% of those who stopped at a display of 24 jams (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000; but see Scheibehenne et al., 2010). A later review found that this feeling of choice overload is more likely when people are unsure of their preferences and when the decision is a difficult one (Chernev et al., 2015). This finding aligns well with online dating.

While having choices ought to feel freeing, abundance appears to make people more rejecting. Across three studies, Pronk and Denissen (2020) found that people grew more rejecting as they worked through a series of potential partners. The chance of accepting a partner dropped by 27% on average from the first option to the last, possibly because satisfaction with partners’ photos decreased and their sense of dating success declined. They describe people as gradually closing themselves off from mating opportunities.

These results are supported elsewhere. Thomas and colleagues (2026) found that among undergraduates using a mock dating app, those who evaluated the largest set of profiles accepted approximately 17% of them, versus about 24% among those who saw the smallest set. Further, viewing more profiles left participants feeling more overwhelmed by choice.

2. Abundance pushes us toward quick judgments

When options multiply, we economize to save brain power. Lenton and Francesconi (2010) report that when people have more potential partners to choose from, they give more weight to traits that can be judged at a quick glance, such as height and weight, and less to traits that take longer to assess, such as education and occupational status. While their data come from speed-dating events rather than apps, I speculate that a dating app pushes the same tendency further, because a photo can be judged in a moment, but much of what we want to know about a partner (especially for longer relationships) takes far longer to learn.

3. Gut-feel swiping can harm how we see ourselves

How we actually swipe on potential partners may also matter. In one experiment, the number of potential partner profiles did not affect self-esteem, but decision style did. Participants prompted to make quick, intuitive judgments reported lower self-esteem and rated their own value as a mate lower than those in the control condition or those asked to make careful, defensible choices. They also began to feel overloaded sooner (Thomas et al., 2026). These findings matter because our perception of our mate value or desirability strongly influences whom we approach. In an analysis of heterosexual users of a dating site in four large U.S. cities, Bruch and Newman (2018) found that men and women typically pursued partners about 25% more desirable than themselves, and the chance of a reply fell as that gap grew. If swiping quickly, off the cuff, using a gut feeling decreases how people view themselves, then I would predict it also changes whom they approach.

4. A profile cannot capture chemistry

Ah, the wondrous spark of meeting someone new and feeling chemistry run through your body, suggesting they might be “the one.” Apparently, it is the one aspect dating models cannot predict. Consider, for example, the findings of Joel and colleagues (2017), who made an excellent attempt to predict connection. They collected more than 100 measures of traits and preferences from participants before speed dates, then used machine learning to predict who would desire whom. The models could partly predict how much a person tended to desire others in general, and how desired that person was by others in general. But they could not predict the spark, and they concluded that this aspect of compatibility is difficult to predict before two people meet. In online dating, it is difficult to know in advance whether there will be chemistry based on what people say about themselves.

Coming next

In my next post, I will look at how this exhaustion differs for men and women and why run clubs may offer something a profile cannot. I will also share some tips for the weary dater. For now, if dating leaves you tired, that may say less about you than about the environment you are dating in.

item.title: “You Can See Everything”: Film Review
item.description:
Social Media

“You Can See Everything”: Film Review

A story of a truly desperate man.

Posted October 21, 2026

Key points
  • Guy Debord foresaw the craving to stage events solely to be seen.
  • Elizabeth Holmes' partner is human click-bait.
  • When does the cost of being seen become too high?

“Whoever is dissatisfied with himself is continually ready for revenge, and we others will be his victims, if only by having to endure his ugly sight.” ~ Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, section 290

In 1967, Guy Debord published The Society of the Spectacle and argued that social life was becoming mediated by images, or what Jean Baudrillard would later call simulacra, with appearing steadily replacing living. Neither theorist lived to see TikTok, yet both anticipated the endless craving to stage events that serve no cause beyond the hunger to be seen.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s mind-boggling and jaw-dropping film You Can See Everything exposes the attention economy as the monstrous theater that it is. You Can See Everything is a true horror film.

The focal point of this desperate attempt to be seen is Billy Evans, partner of Elizabeth Holmes, a man so bereft that he is willing to say anything to be included in the frame. Evans interrupts, steers, deflects, postures, performs, and parades his junk, pouring his energy into making sure that nobody can ignore him. In a scene that Marcel Proust could not have depicted better, Evans steps in to correct the way Holmes limply mixes a bowl of eggs and whisks them with brutal intentionality. This scene will be discussed in film theory classes for decades.

Billy Evans Is Human Click-Bait

The second most revealing scene shows Evans and Holmes in bed with a laptop discussing the resurrection of Theranos in the most egregious Silicon Valley jargon possible – diction that would embarrass every parody, farce, and satire of Silicon Valley. They sound like two people who are trying to join the “cool kids” club by parroting the people already in it. Their performances are blisteringly inauthentic.

The third most indicting scene has Amanda Seyfried baiting Evans into declaring his sexual prowess like a fifteen-year-old boy in a locker room and then watching him angrily vow to ruin the lives of everyone who has wronged Holmes. In Othello, Iago’s motivation remains ambiguous; in You Can See Everything, Evans doesn’t appear to be either sufficiently intelligent or composed to dissemble his aim. He wants to be seen and is willing to test the adage that there is no such thing as bad press.

So the real questions are: (1) What was Holmes thinking when she believed a documentary about these thirty-four days as a docile, innocent, naive, and unrepentant mother would redeem her (and possibly attain a pardon from Donald Trump)? And (2), did Evans think he could outsmart Fielder and Oppenheim and convince the world that he is a business force to be reckoned with while the popular consensus has already labeled him a master manipulator at best?

From the critical acclaim and the online frenzy, it is clear that Evans has secured the audience he craves. In a larger sense, the film is an indictment of our society in general and social media in particular. Journalists have long debated whether naming terrorists rewards them with the very attention they seek: Fielder and Oppenheim have put a megaphone into the hands of a truly desperate man.

If You Can See Everything beats The Odyssey to win the Academy Award for Best Picture (personally, I would vote for Backrooms) and not just Best Documentary, who will have the last laugh?

item.title: Halloween at Every Stage: Balancing Fun, Safety, and Connection
item.description:
Child Development

Halloween at Every Stage: Balancing Fun, Safety, and Connection

Age-appropriate tips for Halloween from a pediatrician.

Posted October 21, 2026

Key points
  • Halloween celebrations need to be age-appropriate.
  • Toddlers benefit from comfortable costumes and short trick-or-treating excursions.
  • School-age children benefit from independence that is paired with supervision.
  • Teenagers need clear expectations, yet opportunities to demonstrate responsibility and independence.

Halloween is a magical event for people of all ages. Candy, costumes, festive decorations, and trick-or-treating create memories that are cherished for years to come. But what excites a school-age child may overwhelm a toddler, and what seems like an appropriate curfew to a parent may feel overbearing to a teenager. Here’s how to make Halloween memorable for people of every age.

Toddlers and Preschoolers

For little ones, Halloween can be exciting and over-stimulating at the same time. Unfamiliar noises, scary decorations or costumes, and the sheer volume of kids running around during trick-or-treating can quickly turn fun into fear.

Start by keeping the celebration age-appropriate:

  • Carving pumpkins needs to be an adult activity. But kids at this age can help by suggesting the appearance of the jack-o-lantern or scooping out seeds.
  • When it comes to costumes, keep them functional: comfortable and secure over elaborate. Make sure costumes do not restrict movement or vision.
  • Skip scary movies and decorations.
  • Have them be an early bird trick-or-treater. Have them collect treats before dark.

When it comes to trick-or-treating, consider bringing a wagon or stroller. Kids this age may try to convince you that they can run around the neighborhood for hours collecting treats. That is usually not the case. In addition, make sure to inspect every treat your child receives before they are allowed to have it. Make sure they understand how many Halloween treats they are allowed to have each day. Check the treats for choking hazards or potential allergens. And, if your toddler or preschooler becomes over-stimulated during trick-or-treating, head home. Make sure your child brushes their teeth well before they go to bed.

School-Age Children

Elementary-school children are ready for more involvement in Halloween festivities. However, that does not mean they are ready to participate in all activities.

  • Pumpkin carving is still a no-no at this age. Knife work is an adult-only activity.
  • Costumes should be night-time friendly. Consider glow bracelets, LED lights, or reflective accessories to increase visibility.
  • Map the trick-or-treating route together well in advance.
  • While it is important to encourage independence, let your child know that you (or another trusted adult) will be supervising all aspects of trick-or-treating. You may walk a house or two behind them, but keep them in your line of sight.
  • Remind children to look both ways before crossing the street, and to use their manners when they are given a treat.
  • Set boundaries when it comes to parental inspection of candy and agree on a reasonable amount of candy to enjoy on Halloween and beyond.

School-age children still need a significant amount of supervision during Halloween activities, especially when it comes to trick-or-treating. But this is also an age to encourage independence. Let them choose their own costume. Let them decide who they want to trick-or-treat with. Encourage them to help parents decorate the house, pick out pumpkins to carve, and provide suggestions for candy to be handed out to trick-or-treaters who visit your home.

Teenagers: Trust, Responsibility, and Connection

Halloween is different at this age. Teenagers may feel too old to go trick-or-treating but still want to participate in the excitement. Don’t discourage them. Teenagers can provide invaluable assistance, especially to younger children.

  • Encourage your teenager to oversee handing out candy and treats to trick-or-treaters who visit your home. This allows them to be in charge so you can take younger kids trick-or-treating around the neighborhood.
  • If teens are going out on Halloween, make sure to discuss curfews as well as approved activities and locations.
  • If your teenager is planning on attending a Halloween party, make sure to have discussions about the dangers of vaping, drugs, and alcohol.
  • Create a plan to get your teen out of a situation they do not feel comfortable in.
  • Encourage teens to be respectful. Taking handfuls of unattended candy isn't harmless fun when it leaves other kids or families hurt or disappointed.

Try to Help Everyone Be Present

Across every age, Halloween can be magical. It provides opportunities to practice important life skills: facing fears, navigating big emotions, managing expectations, developing independence, and demonstrating kindness for others.

Halloween celebrations do not need to involve expensive costumes or full-sized candy bars. What children often remember most is how they felt on this day: included and connected to their friends and loved ones.

Safety matters, but please do not let fear dominate the experience. With thoughtful preparation, Halloween can become a tradition that grows with your family, creating space for creativity, connection, and memories that last long after the candy and pumpkins are gone.

item.title: How Anger Can Take the Fun Out of Life
item.description:
Anger

How Anger Can Take the Fun Out of Life

Reinterpreting frustration can leave more room for play and connection.

Posted October 21, 2026

Key points
  • How we interpret an event helps shape whether we feel anger, fear, or frustration.
  • Reappraisal changes an event’s meaning; suppression hides the outward expression of emotion.
  • Mentally revisiting an upsetting event is associated with longer emotional episodes.
  • Fun involves both pleasurable engagement and a sense of freedom from psychological restrictions.
A pause mid-game: when frustration takes over, the fun drains out of the afternoon.
Source: Travis Tae Oh / Created with GPT Image 2

As the father of two young children entering “teenager mode,” I’ve been trying a small ritual from time to time. We sit down, and I say, slowly, one word at a time, and ask them to repeat after me: “I. Refuse. To. Be. Angry.” Sometimes, it's: “I. Refuse. To. Be. Frustrated.”

This is partly for their benefit. It is also very much for mine.

The word “refuse” needs some explaining. I want my children to be able to tell me they are angry, including when they are angry with me. My hope is that saying the words together creates a pause, a chance to consider what we do with the feeling.

Because anger can take the fun out of an experience remarkably quickly. A game, a meal, or an afternoon together can become entirely about what went wrong (like forgetting to bring something from home, which happens way too often). And then our ability to enjoy the moment seems to disappear.

Why does that happen? And how much say do we have in it?

The Meaning We Give the Moment

Appraisal theory offers a useful starting point: Our emotions depend partly on how we interpret what happens. In foundational research, Craig Smith and Phoebe Ellsworth found that anger was associated with certainty and holding someone else responsible, while fear involved greater uncertainty and a sense of circumstances being beyond human control.

This is the exact example I use to teach about appraisal for my students. Imagine something hitting the back of your head. If you believe someone deliberately struck you and you can confront them, you might feel angry. If you cannot identify the threat or know how to protect yourself, you might feel afraid. These are possibilities, not fixed rules. The physical event alone does not determine the emotion.

The relevant question for a parent would be, “Am I interpreting my child’s resistance as deliberate disrespect? Could there be disappointment, fatigue, or difficulty handling a limit?” I can still hold the boundary while reconsidering my explanation.

In emotion research, we call this cognitive reappraisal. In a classic experiment involving a disgusting film, James Gross found that reinterpreting the material reduced participants’ reported disgust. Simply concealing their expressions did not. Looking calm and changing how we feel are different processes.

This does not mean we can choose every emotion on command but it does suggest that our first interpretation need not be our last.

Then there is what happens after the initial reaction. In two daily-diary studies, Philippe Verduyn and colleagues found that emotional episodes, including anger, lasted longer when the triggering event resurfaced physically or mentally. Duration also depended on the event’s importance and the emotion’s initial intensity.

Fun as liberating engagement: absorbed in the game, free from how it was supposed to go.
Source: Travis Tae Oh / Created with GPT Image 2

Making Room for Fun Again

In my research with Michel Tuan Pham, we describe fun as an experience of “liberating engagement.” It combines hedonic engagement—being absorbed in something pleasurable—with a sense of freedom from psychological restrictions.

That framework helps me understand why frustration or anger can be such a formidable obstacle to fun. When an experience becomes dominated by how it should have gone, how someone should have behaved, or why I deserve an apology, there is little room left to feel free and playful.

Liberation need not mean an absence of challenge. In fact, a difficult game can be great fun. The question is whether I can remain engaged in playing it, or become consumed by my objection to losing or a decision by an opponent. (Catan, anyone?)

Anger can also be useful. Research by Maya Tamir and colleagues found that anger improved performance on a confrontational task. But the goal of an afternoon with my children is usually more complicated than winning a confrontation.

Perhaps there is another question I need to ask myself: How much of my frustration comes from expecting to control the experience?

If I expect my children, our plans, and even my own emotions to unfold exactly as I want, I give myself plenty of opportunities to feel frustrated. I can set boundaries and take responsibility while accepting that the afternoon may have a life of its own.

This brings me back to liberation. Perhaps some of the freedom that makes fun possible comes from loosening my insistence on how things should go. There may be more room for enjoyment when the moment has less to live up to.

“I refuse to be angry,” then, also becomes a reminder to let go.

After all, when I acknowledge that I’m not in full control, anger dissipates and happiness arises.

item.title: Greek Myths and Mental Health
item.description:
Psychology

Greek Myths and Mental Health

Dr. Gillian O'Shea Brown on what Greek mythology teaches us about psychology.

Posted October 21, 2026

Greek mythology has stood the test of time, thanks to its universal themes, storytelling archetypes, and, as therapist and author Dr. Gillian O’Shea Brown, LCSW, writes in her book Psyche’s Awakening, its insights into the human psyche.

From complex family dynamics to overcoming insurmountable challenges, trauma, and suffering to love and relationships, Greek myths have endured through thousands of years as surprisingly relatable stories that reflect aspects of our own modern lives.

Source: Gillian O'Shea Brown/Harper Collins, 2026

Heather Rose Artushin: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Psyche’s Awakening: A Guide to Emotional and Somatic Healing Through the Wisdom of Greek Myth?

Gillian O’Shea Brown: In an era of AI and algorithmic reality, people are starving for what is real and true. Myths endure because they connect us to something larger than ourselves. They aren’t just entertainment—their archetypes are mirrors and roadmaps, reminding us of the resilience and wisdom already waiting inside our own psyches.

After publishing my textbook for NYU, Healing Complex PTSD, I had my own children and realized how much vital psychological wisdom gets locked away behind academic jargon. It made me look back at my own childhood in Ireland, where I understood the world through fairytales and folklore. That’s why I wrote this book: to take the timeless power of Greek mythology and turn it into a practical, modern roadmap for deep psychological healing.

HRA: Greek mythology is having a moment culturally – what about the Greek myths speaks profoundly to the narrative on mental health and psychological healing?

GOB: Yes! I think we all developed a little bit of an obsession with Greek mythology this summer with The Odyssey, but it is not just an obsession – it is a lifestyle. Myths are more than mere stories. They are the original maps to navigate our psyche. They reveal that while the heroes of ancient myths had to slay external monsters, our greatest battle is conquering what lies within.

The truth is, we never truly know ourselves or the strength of our relationships until we are tested by adversity. I’ve come to believe that pain is the elixir the soul drinks to evolve. The hero’s journey isn’t a fictional story; it’s the blueprint of your own life unfolding. It’s a challenging, beautiful path to becoming who you were always meant to be.

Our predestined meeting with our inner "dragon"—whether that takes the form of a painful memory, a deep fear, or a monumental task—isn't an obstacle. It’s an initiation. It forces us to turn inward, face our shadow, and reclaim our power. The archetypal energy of every mythical figure lives inside you. The real magic isn't in a distant fairy tale; it’s your own internal life elixir that allows you to transform wounds into wisdom, pain into purpose, and shame into self-forgiveness.

HRA: How can readers embrace the “hero’s journey” story framework as their own? In what ways do these storytelling models, like those found in Greek mythology, resonate with our individual mental health journeys?

GOB: While in ancient myth, the hero must slay a monster in real life, we must conquer what lies within. Joseph Campbell explained that the hero's journey is not merely an external adventure of battling monsters. Instead, it is equally—if not more—about the psychological journey of confronting one’s fears, doubts, and insecurities: the shadow. Your “shadow” is the hidden, darker side of you—your repressed feelings, memories, weaknesses, destructive impulses, and unacknowledged desires. It is through the confrontation with your "shadow," which can take many forms—the most feared enemy, a painful memory, or an impossible task—that the seeker truly becomes a hero. This predestined meeting with the inner "monster" (shadow) should be viewed as an opportunity rather than an obstacle; it is an initiation that forces you to turn inward, harness power, and overcome fear. A hero's external challenges often mirror their internal landscape.

The very first step to healing is curiosity, followed closely by compassion and accountability. I love what the great sculptor Michelangelo said about creating his masterpiece ‘The David’: 'I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free.' Your authentic self is already inside you, waiting to be unveiled. It is currently buried beneath unresolved trauma, defense mechanisms, and old fears, but within your psyche exists an innate wisdom that knows exactly how to heal. When you stop fighting your fears and start looking at them with curiosity, you unlock a strength you never knew you possessed. You begin to transform your pain into purpose, reshaping your deepest struggles into your greatest source of meaning.

HRA: Which Greek myth do you most identify with, and what have you learned about yourself in the process of studying it?

GOB: The enduring power of myths lies in their ability to reconnect us to something larger than ourselves, inspiring us to live more meaningful and compassionate lives and, most importantly, reminding us of our natural inclination toward doing good. One of the most captivating stories of love in Greek mythology is that of Psyche and Eros. Psyche, the goddess of the soul, goes through trials and tribulations to be reunited with Eros, the god of love. Their story symbolizes the soul’s journey of overcoming trials, aligning with love, and transforming through growth.

In life, we are all on a journey toward sacred reunion, a process of integrating love with the soul. Even the origin of the word psychology leads us back to myth; the word psyche in Greek means “soul,” forming the root of words like psychology (“the study of the soul”) and psychiatry (“the healing of the soul”). And so I resonated most with Psyche — the goddess of the soul: She was not born the goddess of the soul, but became her through trials and tribulations. I believe pain is the elixir the soul drinks to evolve.

HRA: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with your book, Psyche’s Awakening?

GOB: My hope is that this book will help you to live through the pain and emerge on the other side with joy, beauty, and serenity. I hope this book becomes a companion to you and a source of comfort through the dark times. I hope my words shape your internal dialogue as you compassionately witness, rescue, and heal yourself. I hope you’ll share this guidance with others.

I am merely a guide. You are the protagonist, the master, and the hero of your journey. Please accept the invitation to go within and deepen the relationship you have with yourself—to take responsibility for your life.

item.title: When Your Child Outgrows Your Favorite Holiday Traditions
item.description:
Parenting

When Your Child Outgrows Your Favorite Holiday Traditions

What a movie teaches about parenting, change, and making room for new memories.

Posted October 21, 2026

Key points
  • A child’s changing interest in family traditions does not necessarily mean they want less connection.
  • Holiday rituals can evolve while preserving the sense of belonging that makes them meaningful.
  • Creating opportunities for joy works better than requiring everyone to feel it.
Pascale Sutton and Brendan Penny
Source: Hallmark Media

Somewhere, Leslie Knope is enthusiastically approving Pineway’s Christmas market budget. Hallmark’s Mr. & Mrs. Christmas gives us a town holiday project, an ambitious accountant named Sophie Shaw, and the reassuring possibility that municipal work might lead to romance. As a fan of both Christmas movies and Parks and Recreation, I appreciate a story that understands the potential of a well-organized community event.

Beneath the community planning, however, Mr. & Mrs. Christmas raises a question many parents will recognize: What happens when the traditions that make us feel closest to our children no longer seem to interest them?

Taylor Lewis is a divorced father and holiday display expert who moves to Pineway with his two children shortly before Christmas. While helping to revive the town’s Christmas market alongside Sophie Shaw, he also faces a more personal challenge:His teenage daughter appears to be outgrowing some of their cherished holiday traditions and efforts to create a magical Christmas do not go as planned.

The movie’s premise offers a useful way to think about a familiar family tension. A parent wants to preserve something precious. A child wants room to change. Both may care deeply about their relationship while imagining very different versions of a good Christmas.

A Tradition May Matter More to Parents

For a parent, a holiday tradition can hold an entire history. A familiar Christmas movie might recall years of everyone fitting together on one couch. When a teenager loses interest, the parent may feel like that part of family life is over.

Research helps explain why these moments can carry so much emotional weight. In their review of family routines and rituals, psychologist Barbara Fiese and colleagues distinguished between repeated activities and the symbolic meaning families attach to them. Rituals communicate something about who a family is and what it means to belong. Their review linked family routines and rituals with several aspects of family functioning, while also noting limitations in the evidence.

Sometimes we may think we are protecting an activity when we are really trying to protect the feeling it once gave us. Taylor’s family is adjusting to a new home and school. Familiar celebrations could bring reassurance and the feeling that they are still who they always were, even with all the change. The same traditions may carry a different meaning for his daughter, though, especially as she ages. What feels comforting to a parent may feel too young, too public, or simply less interesting to a teenager. Neither feeling cancels out the other.

Growing Up Can Come Up Against Parental Holiday Expectations

One of parenting’s more difficult adjustments is discovering that a child can love you and still decline your carefully planned family activity. A teenager’s desire for more say in family life can be easy to interpret as rejection, especially when a parent has invested time, money, and emotion in an experience. Having a voice and feeling close can be compatible, though.

Research on autonomy-supportive parenting makes a useful distinction between encouraging independence and supporting a child’s sense of choice and willingness. Autonomy support includes taking a young person’s perspective seriously rather than using pressure to obtain agreement. It does not require parents to withdraw their involvement or abandon expectations.

Applied to holiday traditions, that might mean asking kids what part of a tradition, if any, they might still enjoy, if they'd prefer to invite friends to join in, or if there's a specific new activity they'd like to try. These are practical applications of the research, not proven formula for a perfect holiday. Still, they offer families ways to make room for development without giving up togetherness.

There is another recognizable parenting trap in Taylor’s determination to make Christmas magical. He become so invested in creating happiness for his daughter that he leaves little room for anyone to feel something else. Consider the emotional weight of saying something to a child like, but I worked so hard to make this special for you. It may be true but it can also leave a child feeling responsible.

Let Traditions Evolve

It's useful to ask what a ritual can still give to a family. If the answer is connection, there may be several ways to get there. A tradition that once depended on young children’s excitement could now include more of their ideas, skills, and preferences. Such changes may involve some disappointment for parents but it should be possible to welcome a child’s growth and miss an earlier stage of family life at the same time.

The challenge is to recognize that sadness without asking children to become their younger selves to relieve it. Mr. & Mrs. Christmas asks how we can make room for the people our loved ones are becoming, even when we miss who they used to be.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark says: Embracing change can open the door to new traditions, new memories, and unexpected love.

Psychology says: Family rituals can support belonging, and respecting a child’s growing autonomy can make room for connection on new terms. Adapting takes conversation, compromise, and sometimes disappointment. Meaningful traditions reflect the family you have now, with room for everyone to help decide what comes next.

The verdict: Hallmark gets this one mostly right—with a little less certainty about the perfectly timed romance. Making new memories starts with letting the people we love grow and change, even when our favorite traditions need to change with them.

item.title: Be the Book: Focusing on Who You Are While Doing the Work
item.description:
Career

Be the Book: Focusing on Who You Are While Doing the Work

Personal Perspective: What if my accomplishments aren't why I'm here?

Posted October 21, 2026

My literary agent is sending my most recent book out to publishers, and I am waiting to hear whether or not I am a worthwhile human being.

This isn’t how my agent described the submission process to me. What she actually said was that she would send the proposal out to editors she thought might respond to the material. I supplied the part about the response being a verdict of my overall worth in the world.

Because here’s how I feel: If I get a book deal, I am certain I will be able to relax, that my constant striving will settle into a wholesome artistic motivation. I will know that the years I spent working on the book will have been worthwhile. I will stop wondering whether I should have spent those years doing something else. Most importantly, I will finally, finally be satisfied.

I learned a term recently on my podcast Fifty Words For Snow, where my co-host Emily John Garcés and I explore words without easy English equivalents. The term is objet petit a.

Peter Rollins
Source: Used with permission/ Peter Rollins

Irish philosopher Peter Rollins introduced us to objet petit a, a term from the French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan, often translated as the “object-cause of desire.” It’s the thing that keeps us wanting: the elusive something that we imagine will finally deliver the happiness and fulfillment we seek. The problem is the objet petit a, the desired thing, carries a promise far beyond its actual powers.

The book deal is my objet petit a. A publishing house can offer me a contract, but what I’m really asking for is relief from the sense of “lack” in existence. It’s a lot to ask from an acquisitions editor.

The View From Here

Cate Root
Source: Used with permission/Cate Root

On a recent episode of the podcast, astrologer Cate Root joined us to discuss the astrological word retrograde. Cate explained that the word refers to the perceived appearance of a planet moving “backwards.” A planet goes along its orbit, but because of our changing positions as we move around the sun, the planet can appear from Earth to reverse direction against the background stars. Its apparent retreat is the result of where we are standing.

I thought this was interesting because I frequently appear, from where I am standing in life, to be going backward. People younger than me have accomplished things I was planning to accomplish when I was younger than them. Their movement becomes evidence against mine. I can be writing every day and still conclude that I am falling behind.

Kate spoke about retrograde as an invitation to review and reflect. What have we hurried past? What has happened that we haven’t taken time to understand? She wondered why we were so interested in what would happen next when there was so much we hadn’t absorbed about what had already taken place.

For my book, I have spent years investigating something that mattered deeply to me, following questions I couldn’t leave alone, trying to write honestly about experiences I didn’t fully understand. Now I was allowing a handful of responses to my work to determine what all of it had been worth.

A Future Stranger

During the interview, Cate said something I just loved. “What if,” she asked, “my accomplishments are not at all why I’m here on Earth?”

She talked about hoping to write a book that might someday help someone, as opposed to the possibility of helping someone available to her right now. Why should the opportunity to matter always be waiting on the other side of an accomplishment?

Kate told us she came to this understanding while her mother was dying. She had noticed herself withdrawing from moments with people she loved because she wanted to write about them. “Why am I choosing a future stranger that might read my work over this person who gave birth to me, who’s sitting next to me right now?”

Cate said she still wanted to write and connect with future strangers, but that she thought she would have more to offer those strangers if she stayed fully with the people beside her. I thought that was just great and exactly what I needed to hear.

Of course I want my book published. I’ve worked hard on it. I want readers, and I want the particular pleasure of hearing that something I wrote helped someone feel less alone. I love the idea of future strangers and the magical possibility of connection. But I can practice some of what I hope is the wisdom in my book now before anyone agrees to print it.

"Be The Book" tatoo designed by the author's goddaughter Nerys
Source: Used with permission/Nerys Miller-Baynham

Emily and I discussed getting matching “Be the Book” tattoos, an image of an open book with the phrase in calligraphy — an image that could remind us that accomplishments are less important than who we are when doing the accomplishing.

But for now, I am trying to “be the book” without the tattoo. My agent is sending out the proposal. I am waiting. Whatever the publishing houses decide, they’ll be deciding about a book. Whether I am a worthwhile human being was never theirs to answer.
